results.title: Brain region identification
results.question: What are the major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body?
results.response: The major subdivisions of the Drosophila mushroom body are the calyx, pedunculus, and mushroom body lobe system. This information comes from the VFB database, which describes the mushroom body as divided into these three parts: the calyx, which receives sensory interneuron afferents; the pedunculus, a thick axon bundle extending from the calyx to the base of the lobes; and the mushroom body lobe system, consisting of a vertical branch and a medial branch.

results.response: The adult Drosophila brain contains several types of Kenyon cells, including alpha/beta, alpha'/beta', and gamma Kenyon cells. These can be further subdivided into subtypes such as core, surface, posterior, anterior-posterior, middle, dorsal, and others, as stated in the literature (Lee et al., 1999; Aso et al., 2014). VFB holds information on the taxonomy of neurons in Drosophila, including Kenyon cells, as summarized in VFB ref.

results.response: The main input neurons to the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") are projection neurons. This information comes from the literature, specifically from studies on the neural circuitry of the Drosophila brain, such as those by (Laissue et al., 1999) and (Jefferis et al., 2002). According to these studies, projection neurons convey olfactory information from the antennal lobe to the mushroom body, where it is processed for learning and memory. VFB holds data on the neural connections of the Drosophila brain, including the mushroom body and its input neurons, but the specific information on the main input neurons comes from the literature.

results.question: What are the main components of the Drosophila central complex and what functions are they associated with?
results.response:
The main components of the Drosophila central complex include the ellipsoid body, the fan-shaped body, the three paired noduli, the asymmetrical bodies, and the protocerebral bridge. This information comes from the VFB database, as retrieved by the VFB query. 

As for their associated functions, the literature suggests that the central complex is involved in various aspects of behavior and cognition, such as spatial memory, navigation, and locomotion (e.g.,  Wolf et al., 2015;  Seelig and Jayaraman, 2015). results.title: Neuron characterisation
results.question: What is known about the LPLC2 visual neuron type? Where is it, what does it connect to, and what is its function?
results.response: The [LPLC2](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fva "Open LPLC2 in Virtual Fly Brain") visual neuron type is a lobula plate-lobula columnar neuron. According to the VFB database, its cell body lies in the dorsal area of the lateral cell body rind. The LPLC2 neuron has a distinct dendritic arbor in each lobula plate layer, extending outwards from the main fiber in the direction of motion detection for the layer, as described in Klapoetke et al., 2017. This arrangement allows it to detect looming (expansion) stimuli, also reported by Klapoetke et al., 2017. LPLC2 is known to connect to various neurons, including adult cholinergic neurons, T5c neurons, and transmedullary neurons. Its function is to elicit a jump escape response, as stated in the VFB database, summarizing information from Wu et al., 2016, and Klapoetke et al., 2017. VFB holds information on 2,584 neuron types, including the LPLC2 type.

According to the literature, the adult antennal lobe is a bilaterally paired synaptic neuropil domain of the deutocerebrum, and it is divided into approximately 50 glomeruli (Grabe et al, 2016; Ito et al., 2014). The Virtual Fly Brain database also contains information on the neurons and images related to the antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, with [10](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") neurons having some part in it, 10 neurons having synaptic terminals in it, and [911](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") images of neurons with some part in it. 

The documentation from Virtual Fly Brain, specifically the trace containment chain, confirms this hierarchy. The adult cerebrum is part of the adult central brain, and the adult central brain is part of the adult brain. 

In total, VFB holds 10 records of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, 10 records of neurons with synaptic terminals in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, [2](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,NeuronsPresynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with presynaptic terminals in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") records of neurons with presynaptic terminals in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, [8](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,NeuronsPostsynapticHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with postsynaptic terminals in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") records of neurons with postsynaptic terminals in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, 911 images of neurons with some part in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1, and [5](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00003932,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1") records of transgene expression in antennal lobe glomerulus DA1.

results.title: Complete neuron profile
results.question: Give me a comprehensive profile of the giant fiber neuron: its anatomy, connectivity, available driver lines, and relevant publications.
results.response:
The [giant fiber neuron](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00004020 "Open giant fiber neuron in Virtual Fly Brain") is a large adult descending neuron that controls jump escape behavior, as reported by Thomas and Wyman (1984). According to VFB, it has a distinct anatomy, with a large cell body located posterior to the lower protocerebrum, a large descending axon, and dendritic arborization in the antennal mechanosensory and motor center. The giant fiber neuron has a large descending axon that enters the cervical connective via the posterior cerebro-cervical fascicle and descends on the ipsilateral side, in the dorsal cervical fasciculus, as described by Power (1948) and Koto et al. (1981). It arborizes in the ipsilateral zones A and B of the antennal mechanosensory and motor center, where it receives substantial input from zone A and B Johnston organ neurons, as reported by Kamikouchi et al. (2009) and Kim et al. (2020). 

VFB holds information on the giant fiber neuron, including its anatomy and connectivity. Specifically, VFB has [22](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,ListAllAvailableImages "Run in VFB: List all available images of DNp01") images of DNp01, [14](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,TransgeneExpressionHere "Run in VFB: Transgene expression in DNp01") records of transgene expression in DNp01, [361](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,DownstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Downstream connectivity classes for DNp01") downstream connectivity classes for DNp01, and [435](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00004020,UpstreamClassConnectivity "Run in VFB: Upstream connectivity classes for DNp01") upstream connectivity classes for DNp01. 

Relevant publications on the giant fiber neuron include those by Thomas and Wyman (1984), Koto et al. (1981), Namiki et al. (2018), and Sturner et al. (2025), which provide information on its anatomy, connectivity, and role in jump escape behavior. Driver lines for the giant fiber neuron are also available, as evidenced by the 14 records of transgene expression in DNp01 held in VFB. 

Overall, the giant fiber neuron is a well-studied neuron with a distinct anatomy and connectivity, and is involved in important behaviors such as jump escape. VFB provides a comprehensive resource for exploring the giant fiber neuron, including its anatomy, connectivity, and relevant publications.

results.question: Compare the downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons (s-LNv and l-LNv). Do they converge on any common target neuron types?
results.response: The downstream targets of the two main types of clock neurons, [s-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch03yp "Open s-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain") and [l-LNv](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/VFB_jrch0fws "Open l-LNv in Virtual Fly Brain"), have been compared. According to the VFB database, s-LNv and l-LNv have downstream targets and converge on common target neuron types. These common target neuron types include adult interneurons, cholinergic neurons, GABAergic neurons, glutamatergic neurons, octopaminergic neurons, dopaminergic neurons, and serotonergic neurons. Specifically, the downstream targets of s-LNv include adult cholinergic neurons, adult octopaminergic neurons, and adult serotonergic neurons, while l-LNv targets various neuron types including adult CNS neurons, sensory system neurons, and visual system neurons, as found by VFB.

results.title: Novel circuit exploration
results.question: What is the connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body? Could temperature information influence memory formation?
results.response: The connectivity between thermosensory neurons and the [mushroom body](https://www.virtualflybrain.org/reports/FBbt_00005801 "Open mushroom body in Virtual Fly Brain") is supported by evidence from VFB, which suggests that thermosensory projection neurons relay temperature-detecting neurons to higher brain centers, including the mushroom body. This connection implies that temperature information could influence memory formation, as thermosensory neurons may have a plausible influence on mushroom-body memory circuitry through thermosensory projection neurons, as indicated by VFB evidence. The function of thermosensory neurons is related to the sensory perception of temperature, according to VFB. VFB holds extensive data on the mushroom body, including [602](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsPartHere "Run in VFB: Neurons with some part in mushroom body") neurons with some part in the mushroom body, [599](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,NeuronsSynaptic "Run in VFB: Neurons with synaptic terminals in mushroom body") neurons with synaptic terminals in the mushroom body, and [22137](https://v2.virtualflybrain.org/org.geppetto.frontend/geppetto?q=FBbt_00005801,ImagesNeurons "Run in VFB: Images of neurons with some part in mushroom body") images of neurons with some part in the mushroom body, providing a foundation for a narrower follow-up into the relationship between thermosensory neurons and the mushroom body.

results.title: Data availability survey
results.question: I'm interested in studying the subesophageal zone (SEZ). How well-characterised is this region in VFB? What neuron types are annotated, what connectomics data is available, and what genetic tools exist for SEZ neurons?
results.response: The subesophageal zone (SEZ) is a neuropil mass below the esophagus encompassing the three gnathal neuromeres and any regions of the cephalic (supraesophageal) neuromeres situated below the esophagus, as described by Ito et al., 2014. In VFB, this region is relatively well-characterised, with available information on neuron types and connectomics data. VFB contains neurons with some part in the SEZ, which can include image-backed connectome or light-microscopy examples. Additionally, VFB has 4205 genetic tool/expression pattern rows for the subesophageal zone, including GAL4 drivers and binary/intersectional drivers. These resources suggest that the SEZ is a tractable region for study, with a range of tools available for investigating its neural circuits and function.
